idiom_name: key type with restricted construction (friend/private constructor or the language's nearest scope) plus the key as a parameter of the restricted operation
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the restricted type declares an operation that takes an empty key value, and the key type's construction is open only to the designated collaborator - by friendship where the language has it, by nesting where private access is scoped to a class body, and by module, file or assembly scope where the language only scopes to those. The collaborator mints keys and may pass one on if delegation is intended; a non-copyable key forbids that. Keep the key empty and unnamed in the signature, keep every construction path (default and copy) restricted, and state in the code that the boundary is compile-time encapsulation against accident, not a runtime security control.
pitfalls: Leaving any construction path open (a defaulted private constructor on an empty key pre-C++20, a public copy constructor, an exported factory) turns the key into an ordinary argument anyone can supply.
Widening the construction scope wider than the collaborator (package, assembly, module) turns the passkey into ordinary scope-based access with extra ceremony.
Treating the token as protection against untrusted code: macros, reflection, debuggers and patched binaries ignore it because it does not exist at run time.

Wrong move: default or delete an empty key constructor on pre-C++20 C++ -> aggregate initialization can bypass the intended private construction -> instead provide a user-defined constructor body and restrict copy construction.

Wrong move: pass a private-constructor target directly to std::make_unique -> the standard helper has no friendship and compilation fails -> instead use a guarded public constructor with a passkey for make_shared, or explicit local-factory allocation when unique ownership is required.
